extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (practitioners of patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal treatise guidance on what kinds of inventions are patentable (novelty, utility, subject-matter) and how to construe the scope of patents (claims vs description, equivalents, and limitation principles). Includes tests and examples for machinery, manufactures, applications of natural laws, and claim construction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must be new and useful
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act requires that the subject of every patent be 'new and useful,' whether an art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvement on any of these things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry is what constitutes novelty and utility for each category. The statute's requirement applies to all forms of invention and is the threshold question for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must be reduced to practice — no patents for mere abstract theories
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be obtained for a mere philosophical or abstract theory; it can only be for a theory reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is an art it must be actually put in practice and unknown before; if a machine, it must be substantially new in structure and mode of operation and not merely changed in form or proportions; if a manufacture or composition of matter, it must be something actually made and substantially different from anything previously known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty in machinery assessed by mode of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: In machinery, the test of novelty is what is new in the mode of operation: if the principles or peculiar device or manner of producing the given effect are new a patent may be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that a prior machine be identical in every respect to defeat a patent; mere change of proportions will not support a patent. In complicated machinery composed largely of long-known elements, focus on the new mode, method, or application of mechanism to produce a new effect or an old effect in a new way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of old means to a new purpose is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere purpose or effect of a machine, however novel, furnishes no ground for a valid patent unless the machine (the instrument effecting that purpose) is substantially new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application of what is old to a new purpose is not patentable; novelty must lie in the instrumental means or mode of operation, not just in the end achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small amount of skill or accident does not defeat patentability if substantially new
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided the invention is substantially new, it is of no consequence whether a great or small amount of thought, ingenuity, skill, labor, or experiment has been expended, or whether it was discovered by mere accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quantity of effort or intention is not the test of patentability; substantive novelty is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence/principle of an invention is the effect produced by application of natural laws or properties
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a characteristic, an essence, or principle of every invention — commonly its 'principle' — which is ordinarily perceived by observing the powers or qualities of matter, or the laws of physics, developed and put in action by the arrangement of matter, and the effect or result produced by their application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where the subject is form alone, the principle is the result produced via qualities of matter. The principle/characteristic of an invention is often more important than mere arrangement of particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and application of a natural law can be patentable when practically applied
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of nature, property of matter, or abstract rule cannot be appropriated in the abstract, but if an inventor for the first time produces an effect practically by the application of such a law he may, to that extent, appropriate it and claim the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentable subject is the practical application producing the effect; anyone who applies the same law to produce the same effect, however varying means, apparatus, forms or arrangements, practices the same invention — unless the variation introduces a new law or creates a substantially different result. Examples: using expansive power of steam; hot-air blast in iron manufacture; heated-air blast vs. cold-air blast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation of known qualities or laws extends to their application insofar as later applications would be piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions applying known qualities of substances or well-known laws of physical science involve appropriation of those qualities/laws in their application to produce the particular effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee's claim may cover the general ground of applying a quality (e.g., using India rubber to give elasticity to card backs) by whatever form of application produces the effect. The test of extent is whether another's application amounts to piracy of the original invention. But the underlying law or quality remains common property for other, different adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention is generally independent of form; equivalents do not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: When the form, arrangement, proportion, method of construction, or apparatus are not of the essence of the invention, changes introduced in them which do not affect the characteristic or purpose of the invention are immaterial; substituting an equivalent is a different mode of practicing the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when the entire essence and purpose begin and end in form (e.g., manufacture of a sphere for the first time) does form define the invention. Otherwise the invention embraces every application of means that accomplishes the result without changing its nature or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for the extent of a patentee's appropriation: piracy standard under law and logic
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth, law, property, or quality of matter which, by reason of its application, enters into the essence of an invention may be appropriated to the extent of every application which, according to principles of law and rules of logic, is to be deemed piracy of the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation serves as the legal test to mark the extent and nature of the patentee's right: appropriate those applications which would be deemed piracy; leave the underlying properties/laws as common property for other non-pirating uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents should be construed as contracts between patentee and the public
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is in substance a contract or bargain between the patentee and the public on points affecting the rights and interests of either party, particularly the extent of the claim and the intelligibility of the description for practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of the claim is primarily a question for the court; intelligibility of the description is generally for the jury under court direction. Construction should be fair: if doubt remains whether the claim is broader than the invention, presume the patentee intended to claim no more than actually invented. Fraud (claiming more than invented) is not to be presumed and must be proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part inquiry where claim may include pre-existing matter
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a patentee has included in his claim anything that existed before, ascertain (1) whether he makes use of anything not new, and (2) whether that thing, according to the fair import of his language, is represented to be part of the invention he claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether he makes use of anything not new is a question of evidence (unless manifest on the face). The second branch involves applying true principles of construction to the claim language. If doubt persists, construe in favor of the patentee so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual invention where consistent with principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of construction in doubtful cases: favor the patentee (ut res magis valeat quam pereat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, after fair construction, doubt remains whether the claim is broader than the invention, the claim should be presumed to claim no more than actually invented; courts have applied maxims like ut res magis valeat quam pereat to support a patentee where consistent with principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not protect plainly overbroad claims; where a claim is manifestly too comprehensive the presumption does not apply. The practical effect is to support the patent for the real invention rather than to destroy it lightly for uncertain overbreadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent protection covers real inventions but not monopolies over natural laws or properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Law establishes no monopoly beyond the fair fruits of actual invention: it protects the real inventor in what he was first to produce and recognizes as substantive inventions all changes introducing new characteristics, results, or advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation is limited to applications amounting to piracy; underlying natural forces, properties, and laws remain common property and may be used by others for different adaptations that do not pirate the original invention.
